chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Fats Waller the entertainer, his death and his swing organ
summary: Waller would have been a TV star; he died on a train in 1943, and played swing organ at the Lafayette Theater and Connie's Inn.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, you mentioned Fats. We didn't really elaborate --
Oh. Fats was a fantastic, he was one of the most fantastic entertainers. I think if Fats would have lived to the TV era, he would have been a big star on TV. I always have believed this.
No question.
Because he had such a personality and could play. He was very entertaining. He knew just what to give the people.
He was only 38 years old when he died? Is that right?

Yeah, 38, 39. You remember he died when we was on the way to California and he was on the way back. We was on our way, on the way to do our part in 'Stormy Weather.' He had played his part and he was on the way back.
That's right.
And died on the train in Kansas City.
You and I were with Cab Calloway.
That's right.
What year was that, Butter?
1943, April.
Man, you're amazing. Your ability with dates is just phenomenal.
That's right, I'll never forget it.
Well, what about -- anything else about Fats? You know, he did a lot of those piano rolls, didn't he?
Oh, sure, he did a lot of them and so did James P. Johnson.
And who else?
And I think Eubie Blake did some, too,
if I'm not mistaken.
Earl Hines, perhaps?
I don't know about Earl, but I do know about Fats and I know about James P. Johnson doing piano rolls way back there, you know.

And Fats, I have to talk about Fats because one of the great things he did, he revolutionized playing swing organ. He was the first one to ever play swing organ when it was a pipe organ before they even thought about a Hammond. He was playing swing organ then. He used to come in the theater, the Lafayette Theater, and he wasn't working there, he'd just come in between -- he and his buddies would follow him down the aisle and he'd go down in between the picture, or between the stage show and he'd get to swinging and have them people patting their foot and the show couldn't go on.
Yeah.
And then when I came to Connie's Inn, Connie had put an organ for him, a miniature Estey organ in there for Fats to play in between dance sets and the show.
Connie Immerman?
Connie Immerman.
And Connie's Inn?
Yeah, Connie's Inn.
On Seventh Avenue and --
131st Street in the basement.
I see.
And he had an [Estey], a miniature pipe organ, built in there for Fats to play.

Then Fats got so he didn't want to stay on that job. He didn't want to sit down there and play. And sometimes, you know, Fats liked to drink. He liked to swing. He was -- Well, he was a swinger, he was a baller. He liked his friends. He liked to be around his buddies, you know? And he had a lot of buddies. Everybody loved him.
He sure did.
What are you going to do but love him?
Just a happy cat.
Yeah, and he always spread happiness everywhere he want.
Right.
